author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Months ago I sent two deputies to the Maniots. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Maniot deputies: Greece watched from Paris. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il y a plusieurs mois que j'envoyai chez les Maniotes deux députés.

author: The Executive Directory
displayText: “The Executive Directory sees with liveliest indignation Rome's conduct. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Incoming voice: Duphot's murderers shall not go unpunished; Rome next. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le Directoire exécutif n'a vu qu'avec la plus vive indignation la conduite de la cour de Rome.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I received, my dear General, the letters you wrote me. The honor of taking Rome is reserved to you. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Midnight: the honor of taking Rome is reserved to you. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'ai reçu, mon cher Général, les lettres que vous m'avez écrites. L'honneur de prendre Rome vous est réservé.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Enclosed, Citizen Minister, the notes you asked of me. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Cisalpine notes: Mantua, Ferrara to be named. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous trouverez ci-joint, Citoyen Ministre, les notes que vous m'avez demandées.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “By the latest Levant letters, our commissioners offered French mediation to Ali, pasha of Janina. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Ali Pasha offered French mediation via Ionian agents. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Par les dernières lettres du Levant, nos commissaires ont offert la médiation de la République française à Ali, pacha de Janina.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I received your letter announcing your departure for Rome. Arrive as fast as you can. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Hurry to Rome; Mainz army shown off to overawe the Emperor. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'ai reçu votre lettre qui m'annonce votre départ pour Rome. Il faut arriver le plus vite que vous pourrez.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I start to-morrow, Citizen Minister, in order to visit the coasts of the ocean. I shall be back in twelve days. General Desaix is going to Brest, and General Kleber to Havre. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Minister Of War, ^' Paris, 1798-02-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Minister Of War from ^' Paris, 1798-02-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You ought to have received my letters relative to the embarkation of troops at Genoa. Brune has beaten the Swiss, and has captured thirty colours. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Berthier from ^ Paris, 1798-03-10. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Second, to take with me the Citizen Piveron, who was for some tiine enployed as agent to Tippoo Sahib, He might be sent to India in order to re-open relations with that country. […]”
sourceTitle: To The President Of The Directory, Paris, 1798-04-14
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The President Of The Directory from Paris, 1798-04-14. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “On the first decade of Floreal I shall be on board your ship. Have a good bed prepared for me, as if for a man who would be sick during the whole voyage. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Vice-Admiral Brueys from Paris, 1798-04-14. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will be good enough to start to-morrow at 4 A.M., with Citizen Fister, the chambermaid of my wife, and the Citizen Hebert, who will sit on the box with the coachman. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Eugene Beauharnais from Paris, 1798-04-22. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have ordered my couriers to alight at your house; you will see that they rejoin me at Toulon without delay, especially Moustache and Lesimple. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Joseph Bonaparte from Auxerre, 1798-05-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “We have had good and bad weather. We are now well at sea, sailing for Elba. This evening we shall pass Bastia. I have not been sea-sick. Let me know all the news., […]”
sourceTitle: To Joseph Bonaparte, On Board ^ VOriei^t/ 23rd, 1798-05-23
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Joseph Bonaparte from On Board ^ Voriei^T/ 23Rd, 1798-05-23. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Embarking for Egypt, June, lygS. " Headquarters on board the Orient, | " the 4th Messidor, year 6. J " Bonaparte, Member of the National Institute, General-in-Chief. " Soldiers: — You are about to undertake a conquest the effects of which, on civilization and commerce, are incalculable. […]”
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations
context: Embarkation address; month certain, day approximate.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “. I know of nothing more respectable and worthy of the veneration of men than a priest who, imbued with the true spirit of the Gospel, is persuaded that he is in duty bound to obey the temporal power, and to maintain peace, tranquillity, and union in his diocese, &c.”
sourceTitle: To the Bishop of Malta, *'Cn Board the "Orient/ iitk, 1798-06-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: To Malta's bishop, days before the island falls. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Emperor of Russia should thank us, since an occupation of Malta will save his treasury 400,000 roubles. Had his majesty intended keeping Malta he ought to have concealed his designs. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from I'Jth, 1798-06-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Order the Civita-Vecchia convoy before Malta port. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Civita-Vecchia convoy to Malta roadstead orders. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous prie de donner des ordres au convoi de Civita-Vecchia de se rendre devant le port de Malte.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Desaix reconnoitres Malta's coast tonight by galley. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Desaix by galley tonight along Malta's coast. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef ordonne au général Desaix de partir sur une des galères, pour parcourir ce soir la côte de Malte.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Malta attacked tonight: execute orders punctually. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: 9 p.m.: attack the island, execute orders punctually. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef, décidé à attaquer l'île de Malte, ordonne d'exécuter ponctuellement l'ordre.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Duprat instructed to feed your division meanwhile. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Duprat feeds Reynier's division meanwhile. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je donne des instructions au commissaire Duprat pour assurer la subsistance de votre division.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Vaubois lands 2 a.m. somewhere on the coast. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Vaubois ashore 2 a.m. somewhere along the coast. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il est ordonné au général Vaubois de partir le 22, à deux heures du matin, pour se rendre sur la côte.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Eminence summoned aboard flagship over watering rights. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Eminence summoned aboard flagship to answer water plea. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Éminence appelée à bord du vaisseau amiral pour répondre sur l'aiguade.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Midnight: land two 12-pounders at Saint-Julien. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Midnight: two 12-pounders ashore at Saint-Julien. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: À minuit, débarquer à la cale Saint-Julien deux pièces de 12.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will direct citizens Monge and Berthollet to visit the Mint and the treasury of the church of St. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Berthier from 13/A, 1798-06-13. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Egyptians Jb'-, 79- " People of Egypt: You will be told by our enemies, that I am come to destroy your religion. Believe them not. Tell them that I am come to restore your rights, punish your usurpers, and raise the true worship of Mahomet. Tell them that I venerate, more than I do the Mamelukes, God, His prophet, and the Koran. […]”
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations
context: To the Egyptians: liberation proclaimed.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Long enough have Egypt's beys insulted the French nation and heaped outrages on its merchants: their chastisement hour arrived. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Year 1213 of Hegira: the beys' hour of chastisement arrived. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Depuis assez longtemps les beys qui gouvernent l'Égypte insultent à la nation française et couvrent ses négociants d'avanies: l'heure de leur châtiment est arrivée.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Long enough have Egypt's beys insulted the French nation. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Year 1213 of Hegira: beys misgoverned long enough. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Depuis assez longtemps les beys qui gouvernent l'Égypte insultent à la nation française.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Be assured, and assure the Porte, that the same arms we have rendered victorious shall be always at the disposal of the Sultan. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Pasha Of Egypt, Gyzeh, 1798-07-02
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Pasha Of Egypt from Gyzeh, 1798-07-02. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Tomorrow noon: engineers-artillery council at headquarters. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Tomorrow noon: engineers, artillery council at headquarters. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Demain, à midi, il se tiendra un conseil chez le général du génie.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “All consuls' houses currently held are needed for the forces. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Every consul's house needed for the forces: seized. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Toutes les maisons où se trouvent actuellement les consuls sont nécessaires pour les forces.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Every Alexandrian armed within 24 hours of publication. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Every Alexandrian bears arms within 24 hours of publication. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Tous les habitants d'Alexandrie seront tenus, vingt-quatre heures après publication, de porter les armes.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “We have at Cairo, Citizen General, a very fine mint. We require all the ingots which we left at Alexandria, in exchange for the coin given to us by the merchants. I beg you will therefore assemble the merchants to whom the said ingots were given, and ask to have them back. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Written the day of the Pyramids. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I will glYQ them in exchange corn and rice, of which we have enormous quantities. We have driven 2,000 of the best mounted Mamelukes into the Nile. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Kleber from Cairo, 1798-07-21. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Government of Egypt, July 27, 1798. Letter to Tippoo Saib, Jan. 25, 1799. Proclamation to the Army on the Abandoning of the Siege of Acre, May, 1799. Proclamation to the Army on His Departure for France, August, 1799. Part III. Napoleon, First Consul. 67 Proclamation to the French People, Nov. lo, 1799. […]”
sourceTitle: Order on the Government of Egypt, 1798-07-27
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations
context: Occupation organised by decree.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “We have been obliged to spare the inhabitants up to the present, in order to obliterate the terrible reputation which preceded us. To-day, on the contrary, we must assume the tone necessary to make ourselves obeyed; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Menon from *' Cairo, 1798-07-31. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “it was the Justice' coming from Malta. I cried. Fortune, will you abandon me } What, only five days! […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Berthier from Cairo, 1798-08-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “'2 Artillery, with red-hot cannon balls, served with sangfroid, is terrible against vessels. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Marmont from Cairo, 1798-08-02. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have no doubt that by means of Egypt you will 2/ be in a position to make any terms you wish with England. Mistress of Egypt, France would be in the long run mistress of India. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from Wi, 1798-09-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “But what deprives him Q 2. of all chance of recovering my esteem, is his cowardly conduct with the English since he became their prisoner. There are men who have no blood in their veins. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Kleber from ^ Cairo, 1798-09-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “A Portuguese squadron composed of four vessels of war and two frigates arrived before Alexandria on the 29th August, and joined the squadron of cruisers left behind by the English. Render us justice, Citizen Director, for this impertinence on the part of the Queen of Portugal. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Two months in: accounting to Paris. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “*' You will also order the General to seize the property of Hassan-Allah, in order that we may repay ourselves the I 40,000 medins he owes to Koraim. As for the brother of Korai'm, his property should not be confiscated, as he is not yet accused of anything. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Berthier from 6M, 1798-10-06. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I wish you could catch him. I would give 1,000 crowns for him — not that he is worth that, but in order to make an example. It is the same man who went on board the vessel of the English Admiral. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Marmont from 17/A, 1798-10-17. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The barbarous custom of inflicting the bastinado on men supposed to be in the possession of important secrets ought to be abolished. It has long been recognised that this manner of examining men, by putting them to torture, produces no good effect. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Berthier from Cairo, 1798-11-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “He will return along the Nile, and will study the locality so as to be able to form another ambush the day after to-morrow. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Berthier from Cairo, 1798-12-02. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Order Citizen Deriot to march with twenty-five troopers, at 2 A.M., to fort Sulkowski, to pick up thirty men of the 22nd in garrison there, and with this force to enter the village of El Matarzeh, where it is indispensable he should arrive an hour before daybreak, in order to kill some Arabs. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: December night orders: troopers at 2 a.m., Arabs at dawn. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Secret meeting at your house: Perrée, Dumanoir, Barré. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Secret meeting: Perrée, Dumanoir, Barré at your house. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous ferez réunir chez vous, dans le plus grand secret, le contre-amiral Perrée et le capitaine Barré.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Draft every convoy sailor under twenty-five, all nations. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Every convoy sailor under 25, all nations, drafted. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'ai donné ordre pour que tous les matelots du convoi ayant moins de vingt-cinq ans soient levés.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Bon slept at Birket el-Hâggy with battalion and two guns. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Bon slept at Birket el-Hâggy with battalion, Moghrebins, guns. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général Bon a couché hier à Birket el-Hâggy avec un bon bataillon et deux pièces de canon.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Considering the loss we have experienced in the sale of her diamonds, the wife of Mourad Bey must be made to pay 8,000 talari within five days. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Poussielgue from 7M, 1798-12-07. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Coptic nation's letter received; never more debased. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: The Coptic nation protected, never more debased. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'ai reçu la lettre que m'a écrite la nation copte. Elle ne sera plus avilie.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Survey Gizych: villages and influential men. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Survey Gizych province: villages, men of influence. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Indépendamment du myry de la province de Gizych, connaître les villages et les hommes influents.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “No free boats; artillery pays for boats. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: None takes boats free; artillery pays for boats. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Personne n'a le droit de prendre les bateaux; si l'artillerie en a besoin, qu'elle les paye.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “" I was angry with you for revolting. During two months 1 deprived you of your divan; but to-day I restore it. Your good conduct has effaced the stain of your revolt. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Inhabitants Of Cairo, Cairo, 1798-12-21
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Inhabitants Of Cairo from Cairo, 1798-12-21. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Perverse men led some of you astray; they have perished. God has ordered me to be clement and merciful to the people; I have been clement and merciful towards you. " I was angry with you for revolting. During two months 1 deprived you of your divan; but to-day I restore it. […]”
sourceTitle: To the inhabitants of Cairo, Cairo, 1798-12-21
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Proclamation after the October revolt. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “you will threaten him with the bastinado unless he tells you where other Mamelukes and other guns are hidden.,. After which you will cut off his head and expose it with an inscription to the effect that he suffered for having hidden guns. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Verdier from \Wi, 1799-01-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You have already been informed of my arrival on the shores of the Red Sea, with a numerous and invincible army, animated with the desire of delivering you from the iron yoke of England. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: To Mysore: the eastern alliance against England that never was. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Your letter received and read with pleasure. […] […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Your letter read with the pleasure thinking of you gives. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'ai reçu la lettre que vous m'avez écrite; je l'ai lue avec plaisir. […]

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Tomorrow 5 a.m.: foot guides and 100 of the 9th march. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Foot guides, 100 men of the 9th, one 3-pounder double-teamed at 5 a.m. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous ferez partir demain, à cinq heures du matin, les guides à pied et 100 hommes de la 9e.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Back from desert ride: your letters and measures approved. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Back from desert ride: your Frimaire-Nivôse letters approved. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: À mon retour d'une course dans le désert, je reçois vos lettres. J'approuve vos mesures.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Press tax returns by every possible means. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Press in every way the tax returns. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je vous prie d'activer, par tous les moyens possibles, la rentrée des contributions.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Behead Abou-Chayr, divan member, convicted of treason. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Divan member of Qelyoub, convicted: the axe. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef a ordonné de faire couper la tête à Abou-Chayr, membre du divan, convaincu de trahison.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “you will tell them that having learned they have the plague on board, you desire to render them all the assistance dictated by humanity. Send an extremely upright man who is not a great talker and who has good ears. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Marmont from ^' Cairo, 1799-01-09. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain). Trivial OCR repairs (single characters).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Maltese and nautical legions give 10 men each for dromedaries. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Maltese and nautical legions give 10 men each for dromedaries. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: La légion maltaise et la légion nautique fourniront chacune 10 hommes pour le régiment des dromadaires.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Extremely displeased Menou kept the Revanche from Damietta. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Extremely displeased Menou kept the Revanche ordered to Damietta. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je suis extrêmement mécontent que le général Menou ait retenu la Revanche, qui avait ordre de se rendre à Damiette.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Tippoo Sail\ Jan. 25, ijgg. " You are, of course, already informed of my arrival on the banks of the Red Sea, with a numerous and invincible army. Eager to deliver you from the iron yoke of England, I hasten to request that you will send me, by the way of Muscate or Mocha, an account of the political situation in which you are. […]”
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations
context: To Mysore against England.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will place under arrest the officers and sub-officers of the detachment charged to bring in the flock of sheep captured from the Arabs by General Murat, which detachment not only did not prevent pillage, but was the first to pillage. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Berthier from Cairo, 1799-01-26. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Several generals and officers having informed me that their state of health will not permit them to serve any longer in this country, I have given them leave to return to France. The arrival of a vessel at Alexandria with letters for me from Genoa and Ancona has just been announced. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from ^ Cairo, 1799-02-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Write citadel and forts for their returns. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Write citadel and forts for their states. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous voudrez bien écrire aux commandants de la citadelle et des forts pour qu'ils m'envoient leurs états.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Six 6-inch mortars placed at your disposal. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Six 6-inch mortars to Boulaq marine commander. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous trouverez ci-joint l'ordre de mettre à votre disposition six pierriers de 6 pouces.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “General Desaix is 160 leagues from Cairo making excavations among the ruins of Thebes. By the first courier I will send you the levels of the Suez Canal, the vestiges of which are perfectly preserved. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from Cairo, 1799-02-10. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “A Ragusan entered Alexandria with Hamelin and Livron aboard. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Ragusan entered Alexandria with Hamelin and Livron aboard. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Un bâtiment ragusin est entré dans le port d'Alexandrie; il avait à bord les citoyens Hamelin et Livron.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “An engineer at once to the El-Arich road wells. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Engineer at once to El-Arich road wells, watch them. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Donner l'ordre à un officier du génie de partir pour les puits de la route d'El-Arich.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Murat departs tomorrow 27th at 8 a.m. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Depart tomorrow 27th, 8 a.m. (order of the 26th). Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il est ordonné au général Murat de partir demain, 27 du courant, à huit heures du matin.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Bon marches this morning; cavalry too. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Bon marches this morning; cavalry same place. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général Bon part ce matin pour se rendre à la première journée. La cavalerie part aussi.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Pay chest, shoes and clothing all into Fort Qatyeh. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Pay chest, shoes, clothing all into Fort Qatyeh. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le payeur mettra sa caisse dans le fort de Qatyeh. Tous les souliers et effets d'habillement aussi.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Several officers refused to have anything to do with the execution. General Bon commanded the firing party, and his orders (the original exists) were to shoot the prisoners — " taking precautions so that none of them can escape." At the same date (23rd March) we find Nelson writing: […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to M. Sidney Smith from Acre, 1799-03-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The General-in-Chief Bonaparte commanding the armies of the French Republic begs me to inform you that in virtue of the cartel of exchange between the two nations, he sends you the English prisoners captured at Hayfa, &c., &c. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Headquarters cartel letter to his Acre adversary. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Troops burning camp straw and wood on leaving: rarest objects. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Troops burning camp straw and wood: rarest objects. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef voit avec peine que les troupes brûlent, en quittant leurs camps, la paille et le bois.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “" Acre, 8//? Aprils lyc).. Soldiers go out on the roads and carry off the provisions which the peasants are bringing to market; several complaints have been made against the men of Kleber's division. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Hon. William Wyndham, i^rd Ma7, 1799-03-07
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Hon. William Wyndham from I^Rd Ma7, 1799-03-07. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “God is clement and merciful! Bonaparte came to Palestine only to chase tyrants. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: God merciful: came to Palestine only to chase its tyrants. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Dieu est clément et miséricordieux! Le général Bonaparte ne s'est porté en Palestine que pour en chasser les tyrans.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “30 Pluviôse: El-Arich after three days open trench. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: 30 Pluviôse: El-Arich after three days open trench, practicable breach. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le 30 pluviôse, le quartier général est à El-Arich. Ce fort s'est rendu après trois jours de tranchée ouverte.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Take 30–100 Egyptians at Jaffa for a company. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: 30–100 Egyptians taken at Jaffa into a company. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous pouvez prendre 30 à 100 hommes parmi les Égyptiens pris à Jaffa, pour en faire une compagnie.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Sequester every magazine; Gontier to Jaffa. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Sequester every magazine: Gontier to Jaffa for measures. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Faire séquestrer tous les magasins; le citoyen Gontier ira à Jaffa pour les mesures.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “4,000 of the troops of Djezzar were slaughtered, and among them 800 gunners and a portion of the inhabitants." And, *' The Republican army is master of Palestine. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from 13/A, 1799-03-13. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The infamous conduct of the French during the whole war, which they have wantonly waged against all religion and civil order, has at last called down the vengeance of all true Mussulmans; […]”
sourceTitle: To His Highness The Bey Of Tunis, ^Vanguard.' Palermo, 1799-03-14
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to His Highness The Bey Of Tunis from ^Vanguard.' Palermo, 1799-03-14. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “By your description, the castle clearly commands neither the Jordan crossing nor the Damascus road. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Safed castle holds neither Jordan nor Damascus road: staff appreciation. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Par la description que vous lui donnez de ce lieu, il lui paraît clair que le château ne défend ni le passage du Jourdain, ni la route qui de Damas.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I dispatch a vessel to Damietta with army news and General Dommartin's letters. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: A boat to Damietta with army news and artillery letters. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'expédie à Damiette un bâtiment pour vous donner des nouvelles de l'armée et porter des lettres du général Dommartin.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The General-in-Chief will draw from Haifa all the 25th demi-brigade men there, to strengthen Daoud's mill post. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Haifa's 25th men to Daoud's mill; detachments tonight. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: L'intention du général en chef est de faire venir de Haïfa tous les hommes de la 25e demi-brigade qui y sont, pour augmenter le poste du moulin de Daoud.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “On the 13th I sent a boat with a naval officer to tell you our need of war munitions. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Second boat for fear the first miscarried: we need war munitions. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je vous ai expédié, le 13, un bateau avec un officier de marine, pour vous faire connaître le besoin que nous avons de munitions de guerre.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The General-in-Chief orders all your light infantry to march at once for Nazareth. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Light infantry to Nazareth via Chafa-Amr, at once. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef ordonne que vous fassiez partir sur-le-champ toute votre infanterie légère, pour se rendre à Nazareth.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Citizen Larrey will send daily a health officer to serve in the trench. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: A health officer daily in the trench, at its tail. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Ordre au citoyen Larrey d'envoyer chaque jour un officier de santé pour être de service à la tranchée.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The General-in-Chief orders you to march tomorrow at 3 a.m. with the 4th light demi-brigade. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Tomorrow 3 a.m.: 4th light and 25th minus Daoud's men. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef vous ordonne de partir demain, à trois heures du matin, avec la 4e demi-brigade légère.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “General Bon will march at once to take position between Nazareth and Soulyn village. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Bon to Nazareth–Soulyn gap, link with Kléber. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef ordonne au général Bon de partir sur-le-champ pour prendre position entre Nazareth et le village de Soulyn.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Damascus janissaries with Djezzar's cavalry crossed the Jordan to raise Acre's siege; they were completely beaten at Nazareth. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Nazareth and Saron: Djezzar's relief army completely beaten. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Les janissaires de Damas réunis à la cavalerie de Djezzar ont passé le Jourdain dans l'intention de faire lever le siège d'Acre; ils ont été complètement battus aux combats de Nazareth.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “General Baraguey d'Hilliers will weigh from Genoa, weather permitting, on 6 or at latest 7 Floréal. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Sail Genoa–Toulon 6–7 Floréal with casualty returns. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il est ordonné au général Baraguey d'Hilliers de lever l'ancre de Gênes, si le temps le permet, le 6 floréal ou au plus tard le 7.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Abandoning of the Siege of Acre, May, 17 gg. " Soldiers: You have traversed the desert which separates Asia from Africa, with the rapidity of an Arab force. The army, which was on its march to invade Egypt, is destroyed. You have taken its general, its field-artillery, camels, and baggage. […]”
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations
context: Acre abandoned: proclamation to the army.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Scouts hold tonight's right sap, 8–9 p.m. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Scouts hold tonight's right sap, 8–9 p.m. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef ordonne que vos éclaireurs occupent ce soir, entre huit et neuf heures, le boyau de la droite.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Breach great tower untenable under Pharos fires. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Breach great tower untenable under Pharos fires. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le retranchement de la grande tour de brèche n'est plus tenable, à cause des feux du Pharos.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Midnight: occupy the second tower crest. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Midnight: occupy second tower crest by the breach. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Qu'à minuit vous fassiez occuper la crête de la seconde tour, qui tient à celle de brèche.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “March the 22nd light with dromedaries to Hayfa. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: 22nd light with dromedaries to Hayfa authorized. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef vous autorise à partir avec la 22e légère et des dromadaires pour Hayfa.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Move 400 wounded to Tantourah tomorrow morning. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: 400 wounded to Tantourah tomorrow morning. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Faites filer, demain matin, 400 blessés sur Tantourah.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Move wounded to Jaffa or the frigates. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Wounded to Jaffa or frigates; Leturcq sends a convoy. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Faites filer les blessés sur Jaffa ou sur les frégates.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Soldiers, you crossed the Africa–Asia desert faster than an Arab army. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Crossed Africa–Asia desert faster than an Arab army. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Soldats, vous avez traversé le désert qui sépare l'Afrique de l'Asie avec plus de rapidité qu'une armée arabe.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “General Robin marches today at noon for Mesoudyah, resting long enough for soup, water and rest. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: March order: soup, water, rest at Mesoudyah, then midnight march. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général Robin partira aujourd'hui à midi pour se rendre à Mesoudyah, où il restera assez de temps pour que sa troupe fasse la soupe, sa provision d'eau et se repose.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Leave at Qatyeh all Christians sheltered with us from Acre or Jaffa. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Acre and Jaffa Christians sheltered two days at Qatyeh. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous voudrez bien donner l'ordre de laisser à Qatyeh tous les chrétiens qui se sont réfugiés, soit d'Acre, soit de Jaffa, auprès de nous.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The 3rd's 1st battalion garrisons Fort El-Arich until further orders. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: El-Arich garrisoned: sappers, smiths, fifty gunners. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le 1er bataillon de la 3e tiendra garnison, jusqu'à nouvel ordre, dans le fort d'El-Arich.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The General-in-Chief thanks General Dugua for his conduct during the Syria absence. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Dugua thanked: Egypt tranquil through Syria thanks to him. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef témoigne sa satisfaction au général Dugua de la conduite qu'il a tenue pendant son absence en Syrie.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I arrived yesterday with part of the army. I left a good garrison in Fort El-Arich. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Back yesterday; Kléber at Damietta; printed relations hold the truth. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je suis arrivé ici hier avec une partie de l'armée. J'ai laissé une bonne garnison dans le fort d'El-Arich.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “General Desaix goes to Rahyreh province; the nautical legion will leave Rosetta. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Desaix to Rahyreh province with nautical legion via Rosetta. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général Desaix se rend dans la province de Rahyreh avec un bataillon; mon intention est que la légion nautique en parte de Rosette.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I learned with pleasure your occupation of Qoseyr. Engineers are ordered to you. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Qoseyr occupied with pleasure; engineers sent for Upper Egypt works. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'ai appris avec plaisir votre occupation de Qoseyr. Je donne ordre qu'on vous envoie plusieurs officiers du génie.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Yesterday I inspected Cairo citadel myself; Citizen Fauvi takes an improper tone with the commandant. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Citadel inspected in person; Fauvi oversteps with the commandant. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'ai visité hier la citadelle du Caire; je me suis convaincu par moi-même que le citoyen Fauvi prend envers le commandant un ton qui n'est pas convenable.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The General-in-Chief inspected the citadel works; Brigade Chief Dupas's prodigious activity satisfies him. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Dupas praised: prodigious activity, best possible defence. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général en chef a inspecté les fortifications de la citadelle; il a été satisfait de l'activité prodigieuse du chef de brigade Dupas.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Hassan-Toubar leaves me. Tonight he hands over his son as hostage, a man of thirty. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Hassan-Toubar leaves his thirty-year-old son hostage tonight. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Hassan-Toubâr sort de chez moi. Il remet ici, ce soir, son fils en otage; c'est un homme âgé de trente ans.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “May the grace of the Prophet be on you! " I write you this to inform you that. eighty vessels presented themselves before Alexandria, but being warmly received they have anchored at Aboukir and are disembarking troops. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Divan Of Cairo, Headquarters, 1799-07-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Divan Of Cairo from Headquarters, 1799-07-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “There is no other God but God, and Mohammed is His prophet! *' To the Divan of Cairo, chosen among the wisest, the most educated, and the most enlightened persons. May the grace of the Prophet be on you! " I write you this to inform you that. […]”
sourceTitle: To the Divan of Cairo, Cairo, 1799-07-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Governing Egypt through its notables. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Your 3 Messidor letter received, and Friant's of the 12th. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Your 3 Messidor letter; Friant from Beny-Soueyf 12th. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je reçois, Citoyen Général, votre lettre du 3 messidor, et une du général Friant du 12.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Your El-Senytali letter received; all cavalry in Bahyreh. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Your El-Senytali letter; all army cavalry in Bahyreh now. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'ai reçu votre lettre d'El-Senytali. Toute la cavalerie de l'armée est dans le Bahyreh.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Qoseyr customs farmed no more: Suez rules apply. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Qoseyr customs farmed out no more: Suez rules. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: L'affermage de la douane de Qoseyr ne peut exister: même organisation que Suez.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Friant: Mourad still at Hayàn fountain. Drive him out. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Friant: Mourad still at Hayàn fountain; drive him out. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général Friant me mande que Mourad-Bey est toujours à la fontaine de Hayàn. Chassez-le.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Your 19th received; Mourad never left Rayàn fountain. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Your 19th received; Mourad never left Rayàn fountain. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je reçois votre lettre du 19; Mourad-Bey n'a pas bougé de la fontaine de Rayàn.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Both your 18th letters just received. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Your two 18th received at once. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je reçois à l'instant vos deux lettres du 18.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Your two 14th from Talià received; we must gather. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Your two 14th from Talià received; gather a little. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je reçois vos deux lettres du 14, de Talià. Il faut réunir un peu.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “that Corfu had been taken by famine, but that Malta had been revictualled for two years. And in the next letter Marmont was directed to take measures for the defence of Boghaz as "M. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Desaix from Cairo, 1799-08-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Departure for France August lygg. " The news from Europe has determined me to proceed to France. I leave the command of the army to General Kleber. The army shall hear from me forthwith; at present I can say no more. It costs me much pain to quit troops to whom I am so strongly attached. […]”
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations
context: Farewell to the army of Egypt.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have not been well satisfied, Citizen General, with your operations during the movements which have just taken place. No matter what events arise, nothing should hinder a soldier from obeying orders; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Upper Egypt orders, weeks before the secret departure. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Aboukir fort, the enemy's battle reserve, surrendered. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Aboukir fort, the enemy reserve in battle, surrendered. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le fort d'Aboukir, où l'ennemi avait sa réserve pendant la bataille, vient de se rendre.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “8 Thermidor: Aboukir summoned; the pasha's son would yield. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: 8 Thermidor: Aboukir summoned; pasha's son would capitulate. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le 8 thermidor, je fis sommer le château d'Aboukir. Le fils du pacha voulait capituler.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Little satisfied with all your operations in this movement. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Little satisfied with all your operations in this movement. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'ai été peu satisfait de toutes vos opérations pendant le mouvement qui vient d'avoir lieu.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “On Syria return you would pass 150,000 livres to the paymaster. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: On Syria return you would pass 150,000 livres to the paymaster. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous m'avez fait connaître, à mon retour de Syrie, que vous alliez faire passer 150,000 livres au payeur.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Extremely displeased with Zajonchek's negligent execution. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Extremely displeased with Zajonchek's negligence in execution. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je suis extrêmement mécontent du général Zajonchek, qui a mis de la négligence dans l'exécution.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Your 18 Thermidor received; projects fully approved. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Your 18 Thermidor received; projects fully approved. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'ai reçu votre lettre du 18 thermidor. J'approuve complètement les projets formés.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Keep my guides and crews. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. II–V — public domain (French)
context: Keep my guides and crews; Menouf business first. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je vous prie de garder mes guides et mes équipages.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will find inclosed, Citizen General, an order to take over the command in chief of the army. The fear of the English cruisers returning makes me hasten my departure. I take with me Berthier, Lannes, Murat, Andreossy, and Marmont, the citizens Monge and Berthollet. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: The farewell: Egypt to Kléber; France the prize. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “— " We desire a Republic founded upon true liberty, upon civil liberty, and the national representation, and we shall obtain it. I swear this in my own name and that of my comrades. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Laplace from ^ Paris, 1799-10-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I started at once with the Muiron and Carrhe, although bad sailers. I did not calculate the danger. It was my duty to be. where my presence was most necessary. Animated with these sentiments, I should have thrown my cloak around me and have left in a boat had I not had frigates. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Directory from Aix, 1799-10-10. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Citizen Directors, — Since I left France I have received only one of your despatches, which reached me when I was before Acre. It contained the news of our successes at Naples, which made me conjecture an approaching war on the Continent. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Back in France, reporting to the Directory he will overthrow in weeks. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Army of the East. " France acknowledged all the influence of your conquests on the restoration of her trade and civilization of the world. "The eyes of all Europe are upon you, and in thought I am often with you. […]”
sourceTitle: Proclamation to the Army of the East, 1799-11-01
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations
context: Consulate: address to the army of the East.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “*' Foreign to all sentiments of vain glory my first desire is to put a stop to the shedding of blood. Everything leads one to foresee that in the next campaign numerous armies skilfully commanded will triple the number of victims who have already fallen since hostilities were recommenced. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to His Majesty The Emperor from 2Sth, 1799-12-02. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have despatched several vessels to Egypt, Citizen General, and hope they have reached you. I send you a staff officer who will inform you of all that has passed. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Genera.L Kleber from Paris, 1799-12-07. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Courage and virtue preserve states; cowardice and vice ruin them. You have violated hosr pitality. This did not happen among the most barbarous hordes of the desert. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Senate Of The Free And Imperial, ^ Paris, 1799-12-09
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Senate Of The Free And Imperial from ^ Paris, 1799-12-09. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).
